historyItems.originalTitle: Nokia Federal Solutions awarded Department of War RAPID contract to advance multi-domain threat awareness
historyItems.originalSummary: CHANTILLY, Va., 13 November 2026 | 14:00 PM Europe/Amsterdam Nokia Federal Solutions awarded Department of War RAPID contract to advance multi-domain threat awareness Press Release Nokia Federal Solutions today announced that it has been awarded a contract under the Department of War's (DoW) RAPID project, managed by the FutureG Office within the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering (OUSW(R&E)). The award supports Real-World Application Prototyping for ISAC Demonstration (RAPID), leveraging 5G and 6G infrastructure for object detection and tracking. Under the contract, Nokia Federal will develop, build and test integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) capabilities and demonstrate an end-to-end solution for the DoW's RAPID project. The effort supports the FutureG Office's mission by demonstrating how 5G and future 6G networks can be leveraged to improve threat detection and situational awareness, helping protect critical infrastructure against emerging threats. Built on Nokia's AI-RAN platform, the project will integrate Nokia and third-party applications for sensing and spectrum threat awareness. It will combine multiple sensing modalities and sensor fusion to help provide a more comprehensive picture of potential unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) threats. Subcontractors supporting the effort include Nokia affiliates, Texas Tech University, DeepSig, Hidden Level and Future Technologies. " The unmanned system threat is real. Integrated sensing and communications provides the opportunity to help protect critical infrastructure by leveraging the existing cellular networks to identify the threat. This project in partnership with Department of War is helping to advance the technology and the ecosystem to make that a reality. Steve Vogelsang, Chief Technology Officer, Nokia Federal Solutions " " In the FutureG Office, we are accelerating and adapting commercial wireless technologies to meet the requirements of the Department of War, and ISAC is at the forefront of this effort. Through RAPID and related initiatives, we are cultivating an open ecosystem that enables us to leverage commercial cellular infrastructure to bolster force protection and defense of critical assets against evolving UAV threats. Marlan Macklin, Deputy Principal Director for FutureG in OUSW(R&E) " The award reinforces Nokia Federal's role in supporting the DoW FutureG Office's mission by bringing proven commercial innovation into mission-critical environments. It also highlights how commercial technologies can be applied to meet the DoW's most demanding operational requirements. historyItems.originalSummary: A United Launch Alliance Vulcan, equipped with six solid rocket boosters, stands ready for launch at Cape Canaveral's pad 41. The rocket will carry 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Image: Michael Cain/Spaceflight Now. Update: Launch has now slipped to Sunday at 12:11 p.m. EST (1711 UTC) due to a network communication issue between the ground and the rocket that could not be resolved in time for Saturday’s launch window. United Launch Alliance will try again Saturday to launch its Vulcan rocket after a power interruption at a nitrogen plant scrubbed Friday’s attempt, further postponing the 215-foot-tall vehicle’s return to flight after solid rocket booster nozzles failed on two of its first four missions. Liftoff from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is now scheduled for 12:32:30 p.m. EST (1732:30 UTC) Saturday, Nov. 14. ULA said the rocket and the 40 Amazon Leo satellites it carries remain healthy. “The launch of a United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket carrying the Amazon [LV-01] mission is delayed due to a power interruption in the Air Liquide gaseous nitrogen plant which resulted in the loss of their high-pressure pumps,” ULA said in a statement Friday morning. “Without confirmation of sustained commodity flow, the team has decided to realign the launch to the back-up opportunity.” Spaceflight Now will have live coverage Saturday beginning 30 minutes prior to liftoff. ULA announced the delay at 8:41 a.m. EST, a little more than four hours before the originally scheduled Friday liftoff and after the launch team had begun loading liquid oxygen into the rocket’s Centaur 5 upper stage, according to the company’s live mission updates. Gaseous nitrogen is used to purge and pressurize systems on the rocket and launchpad. The one-day delay extends a nine-month wait since the most recent solid rocket booster malfunction prompted the U.S. government to pause its use of the non-reusable rocket for national security missions. The now-delayed mission serves a private customer, Amazon, which has tasked ULA with ferrying 40 broadband internet satellites to expand its Leo constellation. It’s the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon has purchased. ULA has not said how long Saturday’s launch window will last. The rocket will fly on a northeasterly trajectory upon leaving the pad.

historyItems.originalTitle: SpaceX's giant rocket may leave NASA in the dust
historyItems.originalSummary: Later today, SpaceX is planning the most ambitious test yet of its massive new rocket Starship. If all goes well, it will lift off from a pad in South Texas, circle the Earth and then land vertically at the same pad 22 and a half hours later. The test would be a major milestone for a rocket that company founder Elon Musk says he hopes will one day carry astronauts to Mars. But experts say the rapid development of Starship could also end up stranding one of the company's biggest boosters over the years: NASA. That's because as SpaceX ramps up its new rocket, it has said it will stop flying a much smaller one called Falcon 9. Falcon 9 launches the company's Dragon capsule, which is currently the only American spacecraft capable of ferrying NASA astronauts to and from the International Space Station. "Because Dragon has become such a successful and reliable vehicle, it became the de facto way for astronauts to get to orbit," said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space, a firm that tracks the space industry. According to a NASA announcement in September, the space agency has contracted with SpaceX for three additional flights to the International Space Station. That would only allow Dragon to fly through 2028, assuming the missions were flown consecutively in six month increments and no further flights are contracted with SpaceX.

CEO Peter Beck is positioning the upcoming Neutron rocket as a competitor to SpaceX by prioritizing external launch customers alongside in-house programs. The 100th Electron launch and Beck's Neutron versus Starship positioning sit against a wider set of trends our research has uncovered. Our analysis turns up 3 warning signs for Rocket Lab as well. historyItems.originalTitle: AST SpaceMobile presses case for developing own launch vehicle
historyItems.originalSummary: Interested in AST SpaceMobile, Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better. AST SpaceMobile plans to build Blacklift , a reusable rocket designed to carry up to five BlueBird satellites, with a first launch targeted for late 2028 and capacity for as many as two launches per month. The company expects to keep using providers such as SpaceX and Blue Origin for about two more years. Developing Blacklift will require several hundred million dollars in additional capital spending next year , but the company says owning launch capability could eventually cut launch costs by 75% and improve schedule certainty. AST says it is producing six satellites per month and expects 25 satellites to enable initial beta service in the U.S. and several other markets. It also reports agreements with about 60 mobile operators covering roughly 3 billion devices.

historyItems.originalTitle: SpaceX plans over $74 billion investment in Texas, Arizona AI campuses
historyItems.originalSummary: SpaceX (SPCX) pegs its Texas and Arizona AI campuses at over $74 billion, yet the shares barely moved because most of it is planned spending. Arizona is the riskier, larger half: a roughly $50 billion campus filed through shell company Tombstone Resources, with no contract backing promised jobs or bill cuts. A December 9 Cochise County zoning hearing decides whether the $74 billion plan holds or the Arizona half falls into doubt. On November 12, 2026, SpaceX ( NASDAQ:SPCX ) put a single price on its AI expansion. In a company update, it said a supercompute facility at Starbase in Texas' Rio Grande Valley and a campus in Cochise County, Arizona, together represent more than $74 billion in planned American investment.

historyItems.title: 建造火箭很難。 AST SpaceMobile 認為這很「簡單」。
historyItems.summary: 在周四長達一小時的活動中，電信公司 AST SpaceMobile 的創始人兼執行長 Abel Avellan 闡述了他開發大型火箭以將藍鳥衛星送入軌道的願景。阿維蘭一再強調，AST 計劃建造一枚「簡單」火箭。他多次引用 SpaceX 創始人埃隆馬斯克的話說：「最好的部分就是沒有部分。」阿維蘭強調，AST 已經為其擬議的 Blacklift 火箭採購了發動機，並聲稱發動機開發佔典型火箭開發週期的 80%。 「當然，火箭工程師會對我生氣，但你可以將其簡化為一個大型油箱供給發動機，」他談到火箭時說道。
historyItems.originalTitle: Building a rocket is hard. AST SpaceMobile thinks it’s “simple.”
historyItems.originalSummary: During an hour-long event on Thursday, Abel Avellan, the founder and chief executive of the telecommunications company AST SpaceMobile, laid out his vision for developing a large rocket to launch his Bluebird satellites into orbit. Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a “simple” rocket. He paraphrased SpaceX founder Elon Musk several times, saying, “the best part is no part.” Avellan emphasized that AST has already procured engines for its proposed Blacklift rocket, asserting that engine development accounts for 80 percent of a typical rocket’s development cycle. “Of course rocket engineers are going to get mad with me, but you can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines,” he said of the rocket. “So big tanks—we know how to do them. We know how to do them. We know how to do them in composite.” I am not a rocket engineer, and I am not mad at Avellan. But he sure seems to be substantially underestimating the challenge of building rockets. Avellan also has a problem. AST SpaceMobile appears to be successful in building very large satellites, Bluebirds, that are capable of providing direct-to-cell capability from an orbit about 550km above Earth. The problem is there is a commercial launch crunch, and the company is struggling to get its satellites on orbit today, and projects to do so into the future. “We’re not doing this thing because we like rockets,” he said during the presentation. “We’re not doing this thing because we want to be in the launch business. We want this because we have so much demand of our satellites, and as you have seen it, we cannot get enough launches.” The Blacklift rocket will be “simple,” he said, because it will be solely tailored to lift five Bluebird satellites into low-Earth orbit at a time. It will have 20 metric tons of lift capacity, a reusable first stage, and launch twice a month from a pad at Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia that formerly served the Antares rocket. It will have all composite tanks and three stages. And, Avellan said, it will be ready to launch in 2028. If that timeline sounds preposterous, that’s because it is. However, Avellan believes AST has a workaround: It is committed to spending $1.3 billion to acquire enough engines for the first three Blacklift launches from Firefly Aerospace, as well as a license to manufacture additional engines over time. He is basing this argument on the Miranda first stage engine, which he said is “ready to fly.” But that’s not quite true. However, Miranda has not yet completed its formal qualification campaign, much less flown on an orbital rocket. Firefly chief executive Jason Kim said this week that qualification testing remains underway. Moreover, little is known publicly about the readiness of the upper stage engine, Vira, that AST is also acquiring from Firefly for its rocket.
